item.title: Russia vows to intensify strikes, warns diplomats against Kyiv travel
item.description: Russia vows to intensify strikes on Ukraine's military and industrial infrastructure and warns foreign diplomats against travelling to Kyiv ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Greg Sullivan and Olesia Safronova Russia said it would intensify attacks on Ukraine’s infrastructure following a vow from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to double down on strikes against oil refineries, a day after Moscow’s foreign ministry warned that foreign diplomats in Kyiv were in “mortal danger.”  “The Russian armed forces will intensify strikes against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine,” the Russian Defense Ministry said Sunday on Telegram.  The ministry cited comments Zelenskyy made in an interview with Reuters published on Sunday, in which the Ukrainian president said his country had to respond to attacks on energy infrastructure by targeting Russian oil refiners, which “gives money to them for this war.”  The warning came the same day its forces struck the Pivnichnyi, or Northern, bridge across the Dnipro River in Kyiv for a second time, as well as other civilian infrastructure.  Zelenskyy announced the strike Sunday on the X platform, and said Russian forces also hit a pharmaceutical warehouse in Sumy in the country’s north and a communications facility in Dnipro. One person was killed and six injured in the attacks, he said. Russia hit the same bridge, a key artery for the city’s residents, and a logistics center near the capital a day earlier and carried out another strike on Kyiv’s southern road-and-rail bridge last week. Russia said on Saturday that the bridge was being used to transport military equipment.   Separately, Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday morning for talks with Zelenskyy, reiterating Germany’s backing for Ukraine and the dangers posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin.  Hours before Merz’s arrival on an overnight train, Russia’s foreign ministry said it urged “foreign nationals, personnel of diplomatic missions, to refrain from remaining in or travelling to Ukraine.” “Many embassies continue to operate in Kyiv, and foreign officials continue to travel to Ukraine on official visits,” the ministry said in a Telegram post. The “responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” it added.  Last month, the locomotive of a passenger train heading to Warsaw from Kyiv — the main means of travel in and out of Ukraine for foreign officials — was hit by a Russian drone near the Polish border. The strike marked the latest escalation by Russia as acts of sabotage, arson and drone incursions proliferate across the continent. In recent weeks, Russia has intensified its campaign against Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure. Kremlin forces have increasingly targeted residential areas, mail services, and internet and mobile phone providers, in addition to cargo vessels.  Moscow has aggressively attacked Ukrainian energy sites ahead of and during winter throughout the more than four-year war, as it seeks to depress morale and compel Kyiv to accept its terms to end the fighting.  The Defense Ministry in Moscow said recent attacks were “specifically in response to the actions” of leadership in Kyiv, citing strikes during Russia’s parliamentary elections last month as well as during the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June. The ministry also said overnight attacks on the Belgorod region resulted in casualties as well as damage to apartment buildings and private homes.  Zelenskyy told the Financial Times last week that the increase in strikes on civilian targets had come after Putin instructed his military leaders to abandon the rules of war. Zelenskyy cited intelligence intercepted by Kyiv; Russia hasn’t commented on the claim.  “It is important that Ukraine is not left alone against this terror,” Zelenskyy said on Sunday. “Russia must be held accountable for this escalation.”

item.title: How the fashionable Indian was spoilt for choice after 1991 reforms
item.description: Liberalisation brought a flood of international brands into India, but failed to help create a global brand from within the country ...
item.dc:creator: Veenu Sandhu, Sneha Dasghosh
item.content:encoded: India’s affair with the fashion industry started in the colonial era, with the first fashion show, with European clothes and models, held in the 1930s. Post-Independence, after a lull of about a decade, the shows returned in the 1950s with the Spencer sisters — Sylla and Nergish — who brought in the concept of designerwear, choreography and catwalks. That would set the stage for what was to come after India opened itself to the world in 1991.

item.title: Sustained reforms, self-reliance critical for Viksit Bharat, says Das
item.description: Shaktikanta Das said India must build stronger domestic capabilities while remaining integrated with global markets and concluding more free trade agreements ...
item.dc:creator: Krity Ambey
item.content:encoded: Principal Secretary to Prime Minister Shaktikanta Das on Sunday called for continued reforms and greater self-reliance as India seeks to sustain its growth momentum and achieve the Viksit Bharat goal of becoming a developed economy by 2047. “India stands at a pivotal moment in its development journey,” Das said at the Kautilya Economic Conclave organised by the Ministry of Finance. Sustaining the momentum of reforms would be critical to realising the Viksit Bharat vision, he said. Aatmanirbharta, or self-reliance, will be an important part of this next phase, Das said, while stressing that it should not mean turning inward. “Aatmanirbharta does not imply isolation. Rather, it stands for building stronger domestic capabilities while remaining integrated with global markets and concluding more free trade agreements,” he said. India has concluded around eight trade deals in the last five years, most of them with developed economies. It has implemented two free trade agreements (FTAs) in the current financial year and is on track to enforce another with New Zealand later this month. The focus now is on expanding India’s role in global supply chains, strengthening strategic manufacturing and developing critical technologies domestically, Das said. He outlined four other areas that would be key to accelerating growth — harnessing artificial intelligence (AI), deepening the financial sector and bond markets, advancing environmental sustainability, and investing in human capital. On AI, Das called for investment in indigenous foundation models, high-performance computing infrastructure and semiconductor development ecosystems to build sovereign capabilities. As India’s economic weight expands, its financial architecture will also need to deepen, he said. The next phase of growth would require stronger channels for long-term finance and greater availability of patient capital. Das also flagged risks from the global economic environment. With monetary policies expected to remain restrictive and debt levels likely to rise in advanced economies, bond yields could harden further, he said. The current global economy is characterised by wars, fragmentation, unilateralism, technological blockade, energy price volatility and rising inflation, he said. “The interplay of these forces is creating uncertainty across the world, and would perhaps stifle global growth.” Despite these challenges, the Indian economy remains resilient, he said. The Indian economy was also better positioned to absorb global oil shocks, he added. This resilience, built on the back of structural reforms undertaken over the past decade, provides a strong foundation for the next phase of reforms, Das said. “The leap to Viksit Bharat 2047 is very much in the realm of realisation,” he said.

item.title: Uflex, US firm Spectra enters race for proposed polymer banknote programme
item.description: The programme was initiated by Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Pvt Ltd (BRBNMPL), a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: Homegrown polymer science firm Uflex, in partnership with the US-based Spectra Systems, has submitted bids for the proposed polymer banknote programme as the RBI evaluates potential suppliers to manufacture polymer-based currency substrate, sources said.The programme was initiated by Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Pvt Ltd (BRBNMPL), a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).As per the tender document, it seeks Biaxially Oriented Polypropylene (BOPP), coated uniformly with opacifying ink to the required colour, along with an anti-static coating, to provide a good surface for printing and ink adhesion. It requires 68,000 reams, 34,000 each for ₹10 and 20 denominations.Polymer (plastic) currency is used fully or partially by around 60 countries.Australia was the first to introduce it in 1988. Other major nations that use polymer banknotes include the United Kingdom, Canada, New Zealand, Singapore, Vietnam, and Romania.The tender was floated on July 17, with August 18 as the last date for submission of expressions of interest (EOI). The tender was floated after the government's approval to introduce polymer currency on a trial basis.According to sources, a joint proposal from Uflex and US-based Spectra Systems has submitted a bid in the tender.A query sent to Uflex seeking comment on its participation in the EOI remained unanswered.The RBI, with the recommendation of its Central Board, had sent a proposal to the government in terms of Section 25 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, for introduction of one billion pieces each of ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes for field trials and for regular issuance of polymer banknotes in these two denominations after successful completion of field trials, Minister of State for Finance Pankaj Chaudhary said in a reply to the Lok Sabha on July 27.The proposal has been approved by the government, he stated.The introduction of polymer banknotes is currently in a preliminary phase and the impact on digital payments, if any, could be ascertained only after regular issuance of these notes. Moreover, banknotes and digital payment systems are complementary payment tools available to the public, he added.The proposed programme is expected to involve technical evaluation and testing of substrate samples before the larger procurement process. The assessment is likely to examine aspects such as security features, manufacturing consistency, scalability and long-term supply capabilities.The Uflex-Spectra partnership brings together Uflex's polymer manufacturing and industrial capabilities with Spectra Systems' expertise in banknote authentication and security technologies, they added.The proposed programme comes as India evaluates the feasibility of polymer-based currency substrates and the industrial capabilities required to manufacture them at scale.In June, RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra stated that a proposal to introduce polymer currency notes was under consideration by the central bank and was at a preliminary stage.
